facts.fact: India is the world's third-largest energy consumer, after China and the USA.
India's energy use per person is below the world average.
India imports about 85-88% of its crude oil.
India imports natural gas as LNG (liquefied natural gas).
Coal generates about 70% of India's electricity, the largest single source.
Non-fossil sources lead installed capacity while coal still leads generation — a classic trap pair.
India plans to phase coal down, not out, keeping it for base-load.
500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 was pledged at COP26 Glasgow (2021) under Panchamrit.
Panchamrit = five COP26 pledges: 500 GW non-fossil, 50% energy from RE, 1 billion tonne CO2 cut, 45% intensity cut, net-zero 2070.
India reached 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of its NDC.
India's total installed capacity crossed 500 GW in September 2025.
The earlier 175 GW by 2022 goal was renewables-only, unlike the 500 GW non-fossil goal.
The National Solar Mission was launched in 2010.
PM-KUSUM solarises agriculture with solar pumps and farm solar plants.
PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (Feb 2024): rooftop solar for 1 crore homes, up to 300 free units, Rs 75,021 crore.
Gujarat and Tamil Nadu lead India in wind capacity.
A solar park is a large contiguous zone with shared infrastructure where many developers set up plants.
Green hydrogen is made by electrolysis of water using renewable electricity.
Grey hydrogen comes from natural gas; blue hydrogen is the same with the CO2 captured.
The National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023 with Rs 19,744 crore.
The Mission targets about 5 MMT of green hydrogen a year by 2030.
About 125 GW of added renewable capacity will power the Mission.
SIGHT incentivises electrolyser manufacturing and green-hydrogen production.
Green hydrogen targets hard-to-abate fertiliser, refining and steel.
Homi Bhabha's three stages: PHWR (natural uranium) → Fast Breeder Reactor → thorium breeders.
India's thorium occurs in monazite beach sands of Kerala, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.
India has limited uranium but abundant thorium — the reason for the three-stage design.
The PFBR at Kalpakkam, run by BHAVINI, began core loading in 2024 and reached first criticality on 6 April 2026.
DAE bodies: BARC (research, Trombay), IGCAR (fast reactors, Kalpakkam), NPCIL (power plants), BHAVINI (FBR).
Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu) has Russian VVER reactors.
The Nuclear Energy Mission (Budget 2025-26) gives Rs 20,000 crore for Small Modular Reactors.
At least five indigenous SMRs by 2033 and 100 GW nuclear by 2047.
The SHANTI Act, 2025 replaced the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010, opening nuclear power to private players.
India reached about 20% ethanol blending (E20) around 2025.
Ethanol comes from sugarcane, molasses, grain and crop residue — never from petroleum.
SATAT promotes Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) from waste.
BEE is the statutory body for energy efficiency under the Energy Conservation Act 2001.
PAT lets heavy industry trade ESCerts (energy-saving certificates).
UJALA distributed efficient LED bulbs; star labels rate appliances.
PM E-DRIVE (2024) replaced FAME to support EVs and charging.
Battery storage (BESS) and pumped-storage hydro balance variable solar and wind.
India pledged net-zero by 2070.
The International Solar Alliance was launched by India and France at CoP21 Paris (2015), HQ Gurugram.
India leads Mission LiFE, a campaign for sustainable lifestyles.
Andhra Pradesh has one of India's largest pumped-storage potentials.
AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024 promotes renewables, pumped storage and green hydrogen.
Pumped storage pumps water uphill on surplus power and generates at peak — it stores, not creates, energy.
Pinnapuram (Kurnool district) integrates solar, wind and a very large pumped-storage unit.
AP had commissioned about 14,833 MW of renewables by 2026, led by ground-mounted solar.
AP targets about 160 GW of green energy by 2047.
Pudimadaka (Anakapalli district) is the NTPC Green hydrogen hub, about 1,200 tonnes a day.
Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park (~1,000 MW) is in Panyam mandal, Kurnool district.
APGENCO generates, APTRANSCO transmits, APSPCL develops solar parks, NREDCAP is the RE nodal agency.
Anthracite: highest-carbon, best-quality coal (about 80–95% carbon); found mainly in Jammu & Kashmir.
Lignite: low-grade brown coal — mined at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu.
Peat: first stage of coal formation; lowest carbon, high moisture.
Gondwana coal: about 98% of India's coal reserves (Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari valleys).
Tertiary coal: younger coal of the North-East (Assam, Meghalaya).
Jharia (Jharkhand): largest reserve of coking coal used in steel making.
Raniganj (West Bengal): first coal mining in India (1774); first commercial coal-bed methane.
Digboi (Assam): first oil discovered in India (1889); oldest working refinery (1901).
Bombay High: largest offshore oil field, discovered in 1974.
Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin: major offshore gas province off Andhra Pradesh (KG-D6).
Strategic Petroleum Reserves (ISPRL): underground caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur — about 5.33 million tonnes.
Coal-bed methane (CBM): methane gas held inside coal seams.
Shale gas: gas trapped in shale rock, released by hydraulic fracturing (fracking).
Sidrapong, Darjeeling (1897): India's first hydroelectric plant.
Shivanasamudra (Karnataka, 1902): first major hydroelectric station in Asia, on the Kaveri.
Tehri Dam: India's tallest dam, on the Bhagirathi in Uttarakhand.
Bhakra Nangal: multipurpose project on the Sutlej (Himachal Pradesh–Punjab).
Small hydro: plants up to 25 MW — counted under MNRE as renewable.
Large hydro (above 25 MW): declared renewable energy in March 2019.
Brahmaputra basin: holds nearly half of India's untapped hydro potential.
Solar photovoltaic (PV) cell: converts sunlight directly into electricity; usually made of silicon.
Solar thermal / concentrated solar power: uses the Sun's heat — water heaters, or mirrors raising steam for turbines.
Perovskite solar cell: new low-cost thin-film cell material under development.
Bifacial solar module: panel that captures light on both faces.
Floating solar: panels on reservoirs — e.g. Omkareshwar (Narmada, Madhya Pradesh) and Ramagundam (Telangana).
Wind turbine: converts the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity.
Tidal energy: uses the rise and fall of tides — best sites Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kutch (Gujarat), Sundarbans.
Geothermal energy: heat from inside the Earth — Puga Valley (Ladakh), Manikaran (Himachal), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh).
OTEC (Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion): uses the temperature difference (20 °C or more) between warm surface and cold deep sea water.
Low-Temperature Thermal Desalination (LTTD): NIOT plant at Kavaratti, Lakshadweep, uses the same ocean temperature gap to make drinking water.
Fuel cell: combines hydrogen and oxygen to give electricity; by-products only water and heat.
Biogas: mainly methane, made by anaerobic digestion of dung and waste.
Biomass gasifier: turns wood or crop waste into a combustible producer gas.
Second-generation (2G) ethanol: made from crop residue such as rice straw — IOCL plant at Panipat (2022).
National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE): Gurugram, Haryana.
National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE): Chennai, Tamil Nadu.
Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy: Kapurthala, Punjab.
Solar capacity: about 171 GW — the largest renewable source.
Wind capacity: about 59 GW — second-largest renewable source.
Large hydro capacity: about 52 GW, including about 7.4 GW pumped storage.
Rooftop solar: about 33 GW grid-connected.
Total non-fossil capacity: about 308 GW (renewables about 299 GW plus nuclear about 8.8 GW).
Nuclear capacity: about 8.8 GW — the smallest non-fossil share.
India's world rank: 3rd in renewable and in solar capacity; 4th in wind.
Bhadla Solar Park (Jodhpur, Rajasthan): India's largest commissioned solar park (about 2,245 MW).
Pavagada Solar Park (Karnataka): India's second-largest solar park.
Khavda (Rann of Kutch, Gujarat): 30 GW hybrid renewable energy park — set to be the world's largest.
Ministry of New and Renewable Energy: began as a Department in 1982 — the world's first such ministry; renamed MNRE in 2006.
Apsara (Trombay, 1956): Asia's first research reactor.
Tarapur (Maharashtra, 1969): India's first nuclear power station — boiling-water reactors from the USA.
Rawatbhata (RAPS), Rajasthan: first PHWR station, built with Canadian (CANDU) help.
Kakrapar-3 (Gujarat): first indigenous 700 MWe PHWR.
Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu): India's largest nuclear plant — Russian VVER-1000 reactors.
KAMINI (Kalpakkam, 1996): the world's only reactor running on uranium-233 fuel.
PFBR (Kalpakkam): 500 MWe sodium-cooled fast breeder using MOX fuel — first criticality 6 April 2026.
Kaiga: PHWR station in Karnataka.
Narora: PHWR station in Uttar Pradesh.
Gorakhpur (Haryana): upcoming 700 MWe PHWR station (GHAVP).
Jaitapur (Maharashtra): planned with France (EPR reactors) — would be the largest nuclear site.
Kovvada (Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh): planned with the USA (Westinghouse AP1000 reactors).
Atomic Energy Commission: set up in 1948, chaired first by Homi Bhabha.
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE): created in 1954, directly under the Prime Minister.
BARC: began as AEET (1954); renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in 1967.
Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB): nuclear safety regulator, set up in 1983.
Uranium Corporation of India (UCIL): mines uranium; India's first uranium mine at Jaduguda, Jharkhand.
Tummalapalle (Kadapa, Andhra Pradesh): one of the world's largest uranium deposits.
IREL (Indian Rare Earths Ltd): processes monazite beach sands for thorium and rare earths.
Heavy water (D2O): moderator and coolant in PHWRs — made by the Heavy Water Board.
India–US 123 Agreement (2008): civil nuclear cooperation deal; came with the NSG waiver of 2008.
ITER (Cadarache, France): international nuclear-fusion experiment; India a member since 2005.
Bharat Small Reactors: 220 MWe PHWRs offered for captive industrial power under the Nuclear Energy Mission.
Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022: enabled a carbon market — the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023).
Electricity Act 2003: set up CERC/SERCs, open access and licence-free generation.
CERC: Central Electricity Regulatory Commission — fixes inter-state tariffs.
Central Electricity Authority (CEA): statutory technical adviser and planner for the power sector.
SECI (2011): Solar Energy Corporation of India — implementing agency for the National Solar Mission.
IREDA (1987): Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency — lends to clean-energy projects.
EESL: Energy Efficiency Services Ltd — runs UJALA and street-lighting LEDs.
NTPC (1975): India's largest power producer; NTPC Green Energy is its renewables arm.
NAPCC (2008): eight missions, including the National Solar Mission and the Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (PAT).
DDUGJY (2014): village electrification — last village Leisang (Manipur), 28 April 2018.
Saubhagya (2017): electricity connection for every household.
UDAY (2015): financial turnaround of state discoms.
RDSS (2021): Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme — smart prepaid meters, loss reduction.
Green Energy Corridor: transmission lines to carry renewable power to the grid.
National Policy on Biofuels 2018 (amended 2022): advanced the E20 target from 2030 to 2025-26.
PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019): funds second-generation (2G) ethanol plants.
GOBAR-Dhan (2018): turns cattle dung and farm waste into biogas and CBG.
PLI for high-efficiency solar PV modules (2021): production-linked incentive to make solar modules in India.
ALMM: Approved List of Models and Manufacturers — only listed Indian-made modules for government-backed projects.
National Offshore Wind Energy Policy (2015): opened sea-based wind; best sites off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu.
National Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy (2018): wind and solar plants sharing one site and grid link.
FAME I (2015) and FAME II (2019): earlier EV subsidy schemes, succeeded by PM E-DRIVE (2024).
International Solar Alliance (ISA): treaty-based body since December 2017 — first intergovernmental organisation headquartered in India.
One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG): India's proposal (2018) for a global solar grid, pursued with ISA.
keys: One Sun One World One Grid

facts.fact: Global Biofuels Alliance: launched by India at the G20 New Delhi summit, September 2023.
IRENA: International Renewable Energy Agency (2009), HQ Abu Dhabi.
International Energy Agency (IEA): Paris-based OECD body; India is an association country (since 2017), not a full member.
OPEC: oil exporters' cartel (1960), HQ Vienna; India is not a member.
Mission Innovation: launched at COP21 Paris (2015) to double clean-energy R&D.
Simhadri Super Thermal Power Station: NTPC coal plant near Visakhapatnam (about 2,000 MW).
Dr Narla Tata Rao Thermal Power Station: APGENCO coal plant at Vijayawada (Ibrahimpatnam).
Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah Thermal Power Station: APGENCO coal plant at Krishnapatnam, Nellore district.
Rayalaseema Thermal Power Station: APGENCO coal plant at Muddanur, Kadapa district.
Srisailam hydro station: on the Krishna — right-bank station run by APGENCO.
Upper and Lower Sileru: hydro stations on the Sileru, a Godavari tributary.
Machkund: joint Andhra Pradesh–Odisha hydro project.
Polavaram: multipurpose Godavari project with a 960 MW hydro station.
NP Kunta (Ananthapuram-I) Ultra Mega Solar Park: Nambulapulakunta mandal, Rayalaseema — first phase commissioned 2016.
Visakhapatnam Strategic Petroleum Reserve: India's first SPR cavern (about 1.33 million tonnes).
HPCL Visakh refinery: oil refinery at Visakhapatnam.
KG-D6: Reliance deep-water gas block in the Krishna-Godavari basin.
Pinnapuram project developer: Greenko — about 1,680 MW of pumped storage with solar and wind.
